questions.title: Static Method Invocation Without Object Instantiation
questions.question: Write a class with a static method `square(int n)` and demonstrate invoking it directly via class qualification without instantiating an object.
questions.explanation: Static methods belong to the class namespace rather than any specific heap-allocated instance. Declared with the `static` keyword, they are bound at compile time and loaded into the JVM's Metaspace as part of the class metadata. When invoked via `ClassName.methodName()`, the JVM issues an `invokestatic` bytecode instruction. Unlike instance method calls, `invokestatic` does not pass an implicit `this` object reference in local variable slot 0. Consequently, static methods can be executed immediately after class loading without triggering object allocation or constructor execution, making them ideal for stateless utility calculations.
hints: Declare the method with the signature `public static int square(int n)`.
Invoke the method using the class identifier directly, such as `Calculator.square(5)`.
Ensure no `new` keyword or instance allocation is used to call the method.

questions.title: Instance Method Invocation Through Object Reference
questions.question: Write a `Greeter` class with an instance method `greet(String name)` that accesses instance state and invoke it via an instantiated object reference.
questions.explanation: Instance methods represent the behavior of individual objects and require a live object reference on the heap for execution. Declared without the `static` keyword, an instance method receives an implicit `this` reference pointing to the target object as its first hidden argument in local variable slot 0. At the bytecode level, calling an instance method issues an `invokevirtual` instruction, which resolves the method dynamically using the target object's virtual method table (vtable). This mechanism enables instance methods to inspect and modify instance-specific fields, binding behavior directly to state.
hints: Declare `greet(String name)` without the `static` keyword.
Instantiate the class inside `main` using `new Greeter()` before calling the method.
Access the method via the instantiated reference variable using dot notation (`greeter.greet(...)`).

questions.title: Static Math Utility Class Design
questions.question: Implement a `MathUtil` utility class featuring static `add(int a, int b)` and `subtract(int a, int b)` methods, and invoke them directly from `main`.
questions.explanation: Utility classes group related pure functions together under a unified namespace without maintaining mutable instance state. In `MathUtil`, both `add` and `subtract` are defined with the `static` modifier because their computations depend strictly on the provided input arguments rather than object fields. The JVM executes these methods without allocating heap objects, minimizing garbage collection overhead. Modeling stateless domain logic with static methods mirrors foundational standard library designs such as `java.lang.Math` and `java.util.Collections`.
hints: Define both `add` and `subtract` with `public static int` signatures.
Perform arithmetic operations directly on input parameters and return the computed values.
Call both methods directly in `main` using `MathUtil.add(...)` and `MathUtil.subtract(...)`.

questions.title: Stateful Student Display Method
questions.question: Write a `Student` class with private instance fields `name` and `rollNo`, and implement an instance method `displayInfo()` to format and print the student's details.
questions.explanation: Encapsulating state within an object and exposing behavior through instance methods is central to object-oriented programming. In the `Student` class, fields like `name` and `rollNo` reside in heap memory allocated specifically for each instance. The instance method `displayInfo()` accesses these fields implicitly via the `this` reference. When multiple `Student` objects are created, calling `displayInfo()` on each reference outputs that specific instance's attributes, demonstrating how instance methods bind operations directly to encapsulated instance data.
hints: Declare `private String name;` and `private int rollNo;` as instance fields.
Initialize the fields via a parameterized constructor.
Implement `public void displayInfo()` to print the instance variables using `this.name` and `this.rollNo`.

questions.title: Shared Static Counter Incrementer
questions.question: Implement a class with a private static counter and a static method `incrementAndGet()` that increments and returns the shared counter value.
questions.explanation: Static methods have direct access to static class variables because both belong to the class-level scope rather than individual instances. When `incrementAndGet()` executes, it updates a single memory location allocated in the JVM for the class. Unlike instance fields, which exist independently inside each allocated heap object, a static counter maintains consistent shared state across the entire application lifecycle. Static methods provide controlled access to modify or read this class-wide state without requiring instance creation.
hints: Declare `private static int counter = 0;` at class level.
Implement `public static int incrementAndGet()` that applies `return ++counter;`.
Invoke the static method multiple times from `main` to observe the sequential accumulation.

questions.title: Instance Counter Tracker
questions.question: Create a `Car` class that increments a `static int totalCarsCreated` variable every time a constructor is executed, and provide a static getter method to report the count.
questions.explanation: Combining instance construction with static field mutation illustrates how individual objects interact with class-level state. Every time `new Car(...)` is called, the constructor increments the shared static variable `totalCarsCreated`. While each `Car` object maintains its own model and serial number in heap memory, the static counter tracks total instantiations across all instances. A static method `getTotalCarsCreated()` allows external callers to inspect this shared metric directly from the class without needing to hold a reference to any specific `Car` object.
hints: Declare a `private static int totalCarsCreated = 0;`.
Place `totalCarsCreated++;` inside the `Car` constructor body.
Provide a `public static int getTotalCarsCreated()` method to expose the count safely.

questions.title: Static Math Utility Class
questions.question: Write a `TemperatureConverter` utility class with static methods `celsiusToFahrenheit(double c)` and `fahrenheitToCelsius(double f)` to perform pure temperature conversions.
questions.explanation: Temperature conversion is a mathematical calculation that depends entirely on its input parameter and requires no internal state. Implementing `celsiusToFahrenheit` and `fahrenheitToCelsius` as static methods avoids unnecessary object allocation on the heap. By applying standard formulas ($F = C \times 9/5 + 32$ and $C = (F - 32) \times 5/9$) using floating-point literals (`9.0 / 5.0`), the methods perform conversion calculations without truncation, returning clean numeric outputs directly to callers.
hints: Use `(c * 9.0 / 5.0) + 32.0` for Celsius to Fahrenheit.
Use `(f - 32.0) * 5.0 / 9.0` for Fahrenheit to Celsius.
Mark both conversion methods as `public static double`.

questions.title: Static vs Instance Variable Mutation
questions.question: Instantiate two objects of a class. Mutate a static field through one instance, and demonstrate that the change is reflected in the second instance, while instance fields remain isolated.
questions.explanation: This exercise highlights the memory layout differences between instance variables and static variables. Instance variables reside within each object's memory footprint on the heap, ensuring that changing `obj1.instanceVal` has no effect on `obj2.instanceVal`. In contrast, static fields exist as a single shared variable tied to the class in Metaspace/heap. Although Java syntax permits accessing static fields through an instance reference (`obj1.staticVal`), the compiler resolves this access to the class itself. Consequently, mutating the static field through `obj1` updates the shared value observed by `obj2`.
hints: Declare both an `int instanceVal` and a `static int sharedVal`.
Create two instances: `obj1` and `obj2`.
Mutate both fields on `obj1` and print both fields from `obj2` to demonstrate sharing versus isolation.
questions.expectedOutput:
Node1 instanceVal: 50
Node2 instanceVal: 10
Shared value via class: 500
Shared value via node2: 500

questions.title: Non-Static Access Error Resolution
questions.question: Write a program illustrating why calling an instance method directly inside `public static void main` causes a compilation error, and resolve it by instantiating the enclosing class.
questions.explanation: Because `public static void main` is a static method, it executes in a static context without an implicit `this` reference. An instance method requires a live object on the heap to bind its operations and access instance fields. Calling an instance method directly from a static context without an object reference (e.g., calling `display()` directly inside `main`) causes a compile-time error: 'non-static method cannot be referenced from a static context'. To resolve this, the static method must explicitly instantiate the enclosing class (`Solution app = new Solution();`) and call the instance method through that reference.
hints: Define an instance method like `void printWelcome()` inside the class.
Note that calling `printWelcome();` directly in `main` fails to compile.
Instantiate the class (`Solution app = new Solution();`) and invoke `app.printWelcome();`.

questions.title: Static Block Configuration Loader
questions.question: Write a class that uses a `static {}` block to initialize an unmodifiable lookup map with default system codes when the class is first loaded by the JVM.
questions.explanation: Static initialization blocks (`static { ... }`) execute exactly once when a class is loaded and linked by the JVM ClassLoader, before any constructor runs or static method is invoked. This makes static blocks ideal for complex, multi-step initialization of static data structures, such as loading configuration settings, registering drivers, or populating immutable lookup maps. Using `Collections.unmodifiableMap` inside a static block guarantees that the shared map remains read-only for all consumers across the application's lifetime.
hints: Declare a `private static final Map<String, String> CONFIG_MAP;`.
Inside `static { ... }`, instantiate a temporary map, populate entries, and wrap it with `Collections.unmodifiableMap`.
Expose a public static method `getConfig(String key)` to retrieve values.
questions.expectedOutput:
Static block: Configuration loaded.
Environment: PRODUCTION
Timeout: 3000

questions.title: Bidirectional Method Invocation Rules
questions.question: Implement a class demonstrating bidirectional call rules: show that an instance method can call a static method directly, whereas a static method requires an object reference to call an instance method.
questions.explanation: The asymmetry between static and instance contexts stems from the presence or absence of the `this` reference. An instance method executes within the context of an allocated object, giving it access to both its own instance state and class-level static members; thus, calling a static method from an instance method requires no qualification. Conversely, a static method executes without an instance reference. It cannot access instance methods or fields directly because the compiler has no way to know which object's state to target. To call an instance method, the static method must explicitly instantiate an object or receive one as a parameter.
hints: Write a `static void staticLog(String msg)` and an instance `void instanceAction()`.
Call `staticLog` directly from inside `instanceAction()` without any qualification.
Inside a static method like `main`, instantiate the class to invoke `instanceAction()`.
questions.expectedOutput:
Instance action executed.
[Static Log]: Invoked from instance method directly!

questions.title: String Processing Utility Suite
questions.question: Create a `StringUtils` utility class with static methods `isPalindrome(String s)`, `reverse(String s)`, and `countVowels(String s)`, and demonstrate their functionality.
questions.explanation: Stateless utility classes provide cohesive collections of helper functions that operate strictly on their input arguments. In `StringUtils`, each method is declared `static` because string manipulation depends only on the passed `String` parameter, requiring no persistent object state. The `reverse` method uses `StringBuilder.reverse()`, `countVowels` inspects character code points in a loop, and `isPalindrome` compares the string against its reversed form. This design delivers clean helper routines with zero object instantiation overhead.
hints: In `isPalindrome`, normalize case using `.toLowerCase()` and compare with the reversed string.
In `reverse`, utilize `new StringBuilder(s).reverse().toString()`.
In `countVowels`, iterate across characters and check membership against `"aeiouAEIOU"`.
questions.expectedOutput:
Input: madam
Is palindrome: true
Reversed: avaJ
Vowel count in 'Backend': 2

questions.title: Static Instance Counter with Getter Accessor
questions.question: Implement an object tracking mechanism in a `Session` class using a private static counter incremented in constructors and exposed via a `static getActiveSessions()` method.
questions.explanation: Tracking global metrics across independent instances requires combining constructor execution with class-scoped fields. By declaring `private static int activeSessions = 0;`, the counter is allocated once in class metadata and shared by all instances. Each constructor invocation increments this counter. Because the counter is private, external access is provided through a static accessor method `getActiveSessions()`. This enforces encapsulation while allowing callers to query the global instantiation count without holding an instance reference.
hints: Declare `private static int activeSessions = 0;`.
Increment `activeSessions++;` inside the constructor body.
Provide a `public static int getActiveSessions()` accessor method.

questions.title: Static Method Hiding Polymorphic Probe
questions.question: Declare identical static methods in both `Parent` and `Child` classes. Invoke the method through a `Parent` reference pointing to a `Child` instance and demonstrate that static methods do not participate in polymorphic dispatch.
questions.explanation: Static methods cannot be overridden polymorphically; they can only be hidden. When a subclass declares a static method with the same signature as a static method in its superclass, it hides the parent version rather than overriding it. At compile time, the Java compiler resolves static method calls based strictly on the declared compile-time type of the reference variable, not the runtime object on the heap. Consequently, when invoking `ref.identify()` through a reference of type `Parent` pointing to a `Child` instance, the JVM emits an `invokestatic` instruction bound to `Parent.identify()`, bypassing the subclass implementation entirely.
hints: Define `public static void identify()` in both `Parent` and `Child` classes.
Assign a subclass object to a superclass reference: `Parent ref = new Child();`.
Invoke `ref.identify()` to show that the call resolves to the `Parent` method based on reference type.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parent static identify() invoked
Child static identify() invoked

questions.title: Polymorphic Static Factory Method
questions.question: Implement a `Notification` hierarchy with a static factory method `createNotification(String channel)` that returns appropriate subclass instances (`EmailNotification` or `SMSNotification`) based on the input parameter.
questions.explanation: Static factory methods provide controlled instantiation by decoupling client code from concrete subclass implementations. Instead of client code using `new EmailNotification()` or `new SMSNotification()` directly, the base class exposes a static factory method `createNotification(String channel)`. The factory method inspects the channel argument and returns the appropriate subclass instance cast to the common `Notification` interface or base class. This centralizes instantiation logic, simplifies unit testing, and allows adding new subclass types without modifying client code.
hints: Define an abstract class or interface `Notification` with a method `void send(String msg)`.
Implement subclasses `EmailNotification` and `SMSNotification`.
Write a `public static Notification create(String type)` method containing switch-case logic returning subclass instances.

questions.title: Static Method Hiding vs Method Overriding
questions.question: Create parent and child classes, both defining a `static void printMessage()` and an instance `void show()`. Demonstrate the difference between static method hiding and dynamic virtual method overriding.
questions.explanation: This exercise contrasts compile-time static method binding with runtime dynamic dispatch. When a class defines an instance method `show()`, subclasses override it polymorphically: invoking `ref.show()` through a `Parent ref = new Child()` reference uses `invokevirtual` to execute the runtime object's method (`Child.show()`). In contrast, static methods cannot be overridden; declaring `static void printMessage()` in both classes causes the child method to hide the parent method. Static calls are resolved at compile time based strictly on the reference type, so `ref.printMessage()` executes `Parent.printMessage()`.
hints: Define `void show()` (instance) and `static void printMessage()` (static) in both `Parent` and `Child`.
Create an instance: `Parent ref = new Child();`.
Invoke `ref.show()` to demonstrate virtual dispatch, and invoke `ref.printMessage()` to demonstrate static binding.
questions.expectedOutput:
Parent static printMessage()
Child instance show()

questions.title: Thread-Safe Sequence Generator
questions.question: Write a class with a static method `int getNextId()` that provides unique incrementing IDs in a multi-threaded context using `AtomicInteger`.
questions.explanation: Generating unique sequence IDs across concurrent threads requires atomic operations. In a multithreaded environment, standard integer incrementation (`counter++`) is not thread-safe; it involves three separate bytecode instructions (read, modify, write) that can interleave and cause lost updates. By wrapping sequence generation in a static method backed by `java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicInteger`, the `incrementAndGet()` method uses hardware-level Compare-And-Swap (CAS) instructions. This guarantees thread-safe, lock-free ID generation across all threads with minimal contention overhead.
hints: Declare `private static final AtomicInteger ID_SEQ = new AtomicInteger(1000);`.
Implement `public static int getNextId()` returning `ID_SEQ.incrementAndGet()`.
Demonstrate calls to `getNextId()` returning sequential unique values.
questions.expectedOutput:
Order ID: 1001
Order ID: 1002
Order ID: 1003

questions.title: Static Factory Methods Pattern
questions.question: Implement a `ComplexNumber` class with private constructors and static factory methods `fromCartesian(double real, double imag)` and `fromPolar(double r, double theta)`.
questions.explanation: Constructors in Java are constrained by language syntax: they must share the class name and cannot have custom identifiers. This creates ambiguity when two initialization strategies share identical parameter types—such as initializing a complex number from Cartesian coordinates $(x, y)$ versus polar coordinates $(r, \theta)$, where both take two `double` arguments. Static factory methods solve this problem by providing descriptive method names like `fromCartesian` and `fromPolar`. By making constructors private and exposing static factory methods, classes can clearly communicate initialization intent and validate parameters before construction.
hints: Declare a private constructor `private ComplexNumber(double real, double imag)`.
In `fromCartesian`, return `new ComplexNumber(real, imag)`.
In `fromPolar`, calculate `real = r * Math.cos(theta)` and `imag = r * Math.sin(theta)` before instantiation.

questions.title: Static Context Classloader Trigger
questions.question: Demonstrate that accessing a compile-time primitive `static final` constant does not trigger class loading or static block execution, whereas accessing a static non-final field forces JVM class initialization.
questions.explanation: According to the Java Language Specification (JLS §12.4.1), referencing a compile-time constant (a `static final` field initialized with a constant expression) does not trigger class initialization. The Java compiler inlines compile-time constant values directly into the calling bytecode's constant pool, so the target class is never loaded at runtime. In contrast, accessing a static non-final field (or a constant whose value requires runtime evaluation) is an active reference that forces the JVM ClassLoader to load, link, and initialize the target class, executing its `static {}` block. This distinction is critical for optimizing class loading performance and preventing unexpected static initialization side effects.
hints: Create a class `Target` with a static initialization block that prints a loading message.
Define `public static final int CONSTANT = 100;` and `public static int nonFinalField = 200;`.
Access `Target.CONSTANT` first to show no initialization occurs, then access `Target.nonFinalField` to trigger the static block.
questions.expectedOutput:
Reading inlined constant: 42
Accessing non-final field:
[Target class initialized!]
Field value: 99

questions.title: Static Registry Pattern
questions.question: Implement a `PluginRegistry` where plugins register themselves via a static method, and instance handlers query the shared registry at runtime.
questions.explanation: The Static Registry pattern decouples component registration from runtime execution. By maintaining a centralized static registry (such as a `Map<String, Plugin>`), individual plugins can register themselves during initialization without requiring hardcoded dependencies. Application components can then query this registry dynamically at runtime to locate and execute registered plugins by name. This provides a lightweight service-locator architecture that supports extensible plugin systems without third-party dependency injection frameworks.
hints: Define a `Plugin` interface with an `execute()` method.
Create `PluginRegistry` with a private static `Map<String, Plugin>` and a static `registerPlugin` method.
Register sample plugins and execute them via `PluginRegistry.getPlugin(name).execute()`.

questions.title: Polymorphic Verification: Overriding vs Hiding Matrix
questions.question: Create parent and child classes containing both an instance method and a static method. Demonstrate that instance methods use runtime virtual dispatch while static methods use compile-time static binding when called through polymorphic references.
questions.explanation: This exercise illustrates the core difference between dynamic polymorphism and static method hiding. In Java, instance methods use dynamic method dispatch (`invokevirtual`): the JVM inspects the runtime object's virtual method table (vtable) and dispatches to the subclass implementation regardless of the reference type. In contrast, static methods do not participate in polymorphism. The compiler resolves static method calls (`invokestatic`) at compile time based strictly on the declared reference type. When calling a hidden static method through a parent reference holding a child object (`Parent p = new Child(); p.staticMethod();`), the parent implementation executes.
hints: Implement `public void instanceMethod()` and `public static void staticMethod()` in both `Parent` and `Child`.
Instantiate `Parent ref = new Child();`.
Call both methods on `ref` to demonstrate that `ref.instanceMethod()` executes the child's code while `ref.staticMethod()` executes the parent's code.
questions.expectedOutput:
Child instance method
Parent static method

questions.title: Static Nested Builder Pattern
questions.question: Implement an immutable `UserProfile` class with a static nested `Builder` class, supporting fluent configuration, validation, and step-by-step construction.
questions.explanation: The Builder pattern (Joshua Bloch, Effective Java) provides a clean solution for constructing complex objects with many optional parameters. The outer class declares private final fields and a private constructor accessible only to the static nested `Builder`. Because the `Builder` is static, callers can instantiate it without an existing outer class instance (`new UserProfile.Builder(...)`). Each fluent setter returns `this`, allowing callers to chain configuration methods. Finally, `build()` validates parameters and passes the builder's state to the private outer constructor, producing an immutable object.
hints: Declare `UserProfile` fields as `private final` and make the constructor private.
Create a `public static class Builder` with matching mutable fields and fluent `return this;` setter methods.
Validate required fields inside `build()` before returning `new UserProfile(this)`.

questions.title: Thread-Safe ID Generator with Static Synchronization
questions.question: Implement an ID generator using a `static synchronized` method, execute it across multiple concurrent threads, and verify that all generated IDs are unique.
questions.explanation: When multiple threads concurrently invoke a method that updates shared state, synchronization is required to prevent race conditions. A `static synchronized` method locks on the class's `Class` object (`ClassName.class`), rather than an individual instance monitor. This ensures that only one thread can execute any static synchronized method on that class at a time. By synchronizing the ID generation method, increments to the shared counter are serialized, guaranteeing that every thread receives a unique ID without duplicate or skipped values.
hints: Declare a private static counter variable.
Add `public static synchronized int generateUniqueId()` to lock on the class object monitor.
Spawn multiple threads that collect IDs into a thread-safe set, and verify that the set size matches the total generation count.

questions.title: Final Utility Class Pattern
questions.question: Write a `final TemperatureConverter` utility class with a private constructor that throws an `AssertionError` to prevent instantiation, containing static conversion methods.
questions.explanation: This exercise reinforces the definitive utility class pattern recommended by Effective Java. A proper utility class should: 1) be marked `final` to prevent subclassing, 2) declare a single `private` constructor to prevent external instantiation via `new`, and 3) throw an `AssertionError` inside the private constructor to guard against accidental internal or reflective instantiation. All utility methods are declared `public static`. This design makes the class non-instantiable and non-inheritable, communicating its utility purpose clearly to consumers.
hints: Declare `public final class TemperatureConverter`.
Implement `private TemperatureConverter() { throw new AssertionError("Utility class"); }`.
Declare conversion methods as `public static double`.

questions.title: Static Generic Extrema Reducer
questions.question: Write a static generic method `public static <T extends Comparable<T>> T findMax(List<T> list)` that finds the maximum element in any list of comparable elements.
questions.explanation: Static methods can be declared with their own generic type parameters, independent of whether the enclosing class is generic. Declaring `<T extends Comparable<T>>` establishes a bounded type parameter, ensuring at compile time that elements of type `T` can be compared using `compareTo()`. The static method accepts a `List<T>`, validates that the list is non-empty, and traverses the elements, updating the maximum value whenever `item.compareTo(currentMax) > 0`. Because the method is generic and static, it operates uniformly across any comparable type (such as `Integer`, `String`, or `LocalDate`) without casting or code duplication.
hints: Place the type parameter `<T extends Comparable<T>>` before the return type `T`.
Check for null or empty lists, throwing an `IllegalArgumentException` if invalid.
Iterate through the list comparing elements using `item.compareTo(max)`.

questions.title: Static Memory Leak and Cache Eviction
questions.question: Demonstrate an unintentional memory leak caused by an unbounded static collection cache, and implement an eviction policy using `LinkedHashMap` to bound cache size.
questions.explanation: Static collections represent a common source of memory leaks in Java applications. Because static fields are rooted in class metadata, they act as permanent GC roots that remain alive for the lifetime of the JVM ClassLoader. If objects are continuously added to a static collection without removal, the Garbage Collector cannot reclaim them, eventually causing an `OutOfMemoryError: Java heap space`. To fix this, caches must enforce bounded eviction policies. By extending `LinkedHashMap` and overriding `removeEldestEntry()`, the cache automatically evicts the oldest entry when size exceeds a threshold, keeping heap consumption bounded.
hints: Explain that static collections act as permanent GC roots that prevent garbage collection.
Implement a bounded LRU cache using `new LinkedHashMap<K, V>(capacity, 0.75f, true)`.
Override `protected boolean removeEldestEntry(Map.Entry eldest)` to return `size() > MAX_CAPACITY`.
questions.expectedOutput:
Cache contents: {B=Beta, C=Gamma}
Contains evicted key 'A': false

questions.title: Static Initialization Class Deadlock
questions.question: Construct a two-thread static class initialization deadlock scenario where class `A`'s static block depends on class `B`, while class `B`'s static block depends on class `A`.
questions.explanation: During class initialization, the JVM acquires a unique initialization lock on the target class's `Class` object (JLS §12.4.2) to ensure thread-safe initialization. If class `A`'s static initialization block spawns or waits on a thread that references class `B`, while class `B`'s static initialization block simultaneously references class `A`, both threads block waiting for each other's initialization locks. Thread 1 holds the lock on `A` and waits for `B` to initialize; Thread 2 holds the lock on `B` and waits for `A` to initialize. This produces a static initialization deadlock that completely halts execution without throwing an exception.
hints: In class `A`'s static block, start a thread that references `B.initFlag`.
In class `B`'s static block, reference `A.initFlag` to create a circular dependency.
Document that JVM class initialization uses internal locks on the `Class` object, which can deadlock when static dependencies are circular.
questions.expectedOutput:
Triggering NodeB:
NodeB: static block started
NodeA: static block started
NodeA: initialized successfully
NodeB: initialized successfully
Result: 15

questions.title: Mocking Static Dependencies via Supplier Injection
questions.question: Implement an architecture pattern using supplier injection that allows unit testing code dependent on a system clock (`System.currentTimeMillis()`) without relying on static mocking libraries.
questions.explanation: Hardcoding direct calls to static methods like `System.currentTimeMillis()` creates tightly coupled code that is difficult to unit test, because test cases cannot control the current time to verify timeouts or expiration logic. Rather than using bytecode manipulation tools (such as PowerMock), a clean design pattern injects a functional supplier (`LongSupplier` or `java.time.Clock`). In production, the service defaults to `System::currentTimeMillis`. During testing, test code injects a mock supplier that returns fixed timestamps, enabling deterministic verification of time-dependent logic without external libraries.
hints: Define a `LongSupplier timeProvider` field inside the service class.
Provide a default constructor setting `this.timeProvider = System::currentTimeMillis;`.
Provide a package-private constructor accepting a custom `LongSupplier` for testing.
questions.expectedOutput: Is token expired at mock time: true

questions.title: Singleton with Double-Checked Locking
questions.question: Implement the Double-Checked Locking singleton pattern using a `private static volatile` instance variable and synchronized block, and explain why the `volatile` modifier is required.
questions.explanation: The Double-Checked Locking pattern provides thread-safe lazy initialization while avoiding synchronization overhead on reads after the instance is created. The method checks `if (instance == null)` first; if null, it acquires a `synchronized` lock on the class and checks again before instantiating. The `volatile` modifier on `instance` is required to prevent CPU and compiler instruction reordering. Without `volatile`, the JVM could reorder the steps of object construction (allocating memory, assigning the reference, and running the constructor), allowing another thread to observe a non-null but uninitialized object reference.
hints: Declare `private static volatile Singleton instance;`.
Check `if (instance == null)` before entering the synchronized block, then check again inside.
Explain that `volatile` introduces memory barriers that prevent instruction reordering during construction.
questions.expectedOutput:
Singleton identity check: true
Status: Connected to Database

questions.title: Static Polymorphism via Curiously Recurring Pattern
questions.question: Simulate static polymorphism in Java using generic self-referential bounds (Curiously Recurring Template Pattern) to achieve fluent builder inheritance without dynamic virtual table dispatch.
questions.explanation: In standard Java inheritance, method chaining breaks when a subclass calls a method inherited from a parent builder: the parent method returns a parent builder reference, preventing subsequent subclass methods from being called without explicit casting. The Curiously Recurring Template Pattern (CRTP) solves this at compile time using self-referential generics: `abstract class Builder<T extends Builder<T>>`. Parent methods return `self()`, which returns `(T) this`. Subclasses bind `T` to their own type, allowing subclass methods to be chained after parent builder methods without virtual method dispatch or runtime downcasting.
hints: Define `abstract static class Builder<T extends Builder<T>>` with a protected `abstract T self();` method.
Have parent builder methods return `T` by returning `self()`.
Extend the builder in a subclass: `static class ConcreteBuilder extends Builder<ConcreteBuilder>` and implement `self() { return this; }`.
